title: DECISION: ranking-query p99 latency SLO is the re-evaluation trigger, not row count
description:
## Context
plan.md "Leaderboard snapshot sizing" section (~lines 1008-1029): "No re-evaluation trigger is defined for 'Postgres computes ranking directly' past current scale... This plan does not state a row-count or query-latency threshold at which the direct-SQL-ranking approach should be revisited." "**Adopted (2026-08-04, plan-idea-gen run 1): the trigger is a measured query-latency SLO, not a row count.** Row count was the more obvious choice but is a proxy for the thing that actually matters — pick one number now (e.g., the ranking query's p99 latency staying under 2s) and monitor it; when it's breached, that's the signal to build the materialized/precomputed ranking table this section already names as the fallback, not before. This deliberately doesn't build that materialization now."

## Task
Record the concrete SLO number (e.g. AGG-CORE ranking query p99 < 2s, measured over each 15-minute cycle) as the sole re-evaluation trigger for moving off direct-Postgres-SQL ranking to a materialized/precomputed ranking table. Explicitly state: do not build the materialized table now; it is built only if/when this SLO is breached.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A specific, numeric SLO is documented (e.g. "ranking query p99 < 2s over trailing N cycles").
- [ ] Doc explicitly states the materialized ranking table is NOT built as part of this work — it is a future action gated on SLO breach.
- [ ] Row count is explicitly documented as *not* the trigger, to prevent a future contributor reintroducing a row-count-based trigger by default.
close_reason: Completed

description:

measurement`, item 4: "The largest repo is a fixture. Whatever the
measurement finds as the corpus maximum becomes a named test case,
exercised end-to-end before Phase 5, not discovered in production." Also
`### ARMOR storage sizing`: "Sample the tail, not the mean ... The sample
must include the corpus's actual largest repos by commit count."

## Task
Once the Phase 0 ARMOR stratified-sample measurement identifies the
corpus's largest repo(s) by commit count, build a durable, named test
fixture (real repo clone, or a synthetic repo of equivalent scale if the
real one is impractical to check into CI) and run it end-to-end through
clone-worker: full clone, extraction, detection, quarantine, rollup write,
Parquet write, and warm-start artifact write — asserting the extremes
hardening beads (streaming Parquet, warm-start ceiling, bounded
transaction) all activate correctly at this scale.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Fixture is named and checked into the test suite (or its provenance/regeneration procedure is documented if too large to check in directly).
- [ ] End-to-end run stays within a stated memory ceiling for the clone-worker pod.
- [ ] If the fixture's warm-start artifact exceeds the configured ceiling (`cw-extremes-warmstart-ceiling`), the test confirms it is skipped and full-clone-fallback is used on the next run, without failing the job.
- [ ] If the fixture's rollup row count exceeds the chunking threshold (`cw-extremes-bounded-transaction`), the test confirms multiple bounded transactions were used and the final state matches a single-transaction-equivalent result.
- [ ] This test runs before Phase 5 (discovery restart) per the plan's explicit sequencing.

title: Test: alias merge before RANK() changes totals and rank correctly
description:
## Context
plan.md "### Identity lives in Postgres, not queue-api" (~lines 391-410): "When one person's commits sit under two email keys, ranking before the merge produces two wrong rows, and merging afterward changes their totals — which changes their rank, and everyone else's. Rank must be computed *after* alias resolution."

## Task
Write an automated test against a seeded fixture database proving the ordering is correct: create two `email_resolution` rows pointing at the same login (and/or a `user_aliases` row merging two logins), each with rollup commits, and assert the merged row's `ai_commits_30d`/rank reflects the sum — not two separate ranked rows, and not a rank computed pre-merge then patched.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Fixture: two emails resolving to one canonical login, each contributing commits in the 30-day window.
- [ ] Test asserts exactly one ranked row exists for the canonical login with summed `ai_commits_30d`.
- [ ] Test asserts the merged row's rank reflects its summed total relative to other rows' totals — the test must be able to fail if merge happened after RANK() instead of before.
- [ ] Test added to CI (Argo Workflows on iad-ci), not a manual-only check.

title: Implement bulk-upsert identity ingest path with the source/resolved_at conflict rule
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### Identity ingest endpoint": "Every row carries a
**`source`** (`live` / `seed` / `manual`) and a **`resolved_at`**. Conflict
resolution is then a single rule":

```sql
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE
  SET login = excluded.login, source = excluded.source,
      resolved_at = excluded.resolved_at
  WHERE excluded.source = 'manual'
     OR (email_resolution.source <> 'manual'
         AND excluded.resolved_at > email_resolution.resolved_at)
```

"This is strictly better than the pending-only rule an earlier draft
specified. A seed that is 5-8+ weeks stale by the time it runs can never beat
a live result; hand curation is never clobbered by either; the operation is
naturally idempotent; and because `source` is retained, every row's
provenance stays auditable."

## Task
Implement this exact upsert as the one bulk-upsert path all three writers
(live enrichment worker, claude-leaderboard seed, manual curation) go
through — accepting a batch of `(email, login, source, resolved_at)` rows
and applying the `ON CONFLICT` rule verbatim.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Accepts a batch of rows (not row-at-a-time only — the seed alone is
      349,425 rows and must not require 349,425 round trips).
- [ ] `ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE ... WHERE` clause matches the plan's
      SQL exactly — a manual source always wins; otherwise the existing row
      wins unless the new row is non-manual AND strictly newer by
      `resolved_at`.
- [ ] A row that loses the conflict check is silently skipped for that email
      (not an error) — this is upsert semantics, not an all-or-nothing
      batch failure.
- [ ] Function/endpoint is the single path all three writers use — no writer
      is allowed a raw `INSERT`/`UPDATE` against `email_resolution` that
      bypasses this rule.
close_reason: Completed

identity.** Every `user_id` in the rollup resolves to a `users` row; every
`user_aliases.target_login` exists in `users`; the alias graph is acyclic
and one level deep (no alias whose target is itself an alias source)." This
is one of the explicitly required test beads for this project.

## Task
Write SQL assertions and CI tests covering the full invariant, using both
the `admin`-reason rows from `user-aliases-seed-admin-configmap` and
synthetic `name-match`-reason rows.

- [ ] Test asserts every `user_aliases.target_login` exists as a

      confirm it's rejected or flagged (decide and document whether this is

title: Locate commit parsing code
description:

notes:
Completed search for commit parsing code.

Key findings:
- This codebase does NOT contain native Go git commit parsing functions
- Uses external git commands via os/exec instead
- Primary location: pkg/warmstart/extract.go
- Key functions:
  * ParseTarball() - Entry point for parsing warm-start tarballs containing git pack files
  * Materialize() - Writes git pack files and refs
  * VerifyGitFsck() - Runs 'git fsck --no-full --no-progress' 
  * VerifyGitLog() - Runs 'git log --oneline -n 1'
  * RunSanityChecks() - Runs both verifications

Git commands executed:
- exec.Command('git', '--git-dir='+gitDir, 'fsck', '--no-full', '--no-progress')
- exec.Command('git', '--git-dir='+gitDir, 'log', '--oneline', '-n', '1')

Supporting files:
- pkg/errors/helpers.go - Commit-related error handling
- pkg/rollup/rollup.go - Commit struct for processing (not parsing)

Conclusion: Project focuses on git repository materialization and verification rather than native commit parsing. Actual git commit parsing happens through external git commands.
close_reason: Successfully located commit parsing code. Found that this codebase uses external git commands (via os/exec) rather than native Go parsing. Primary location is pkg/warmstart/extract.go with functions like ParseTarball(), VerifyGitFsck(), and VerifyGitLog() that execute git commands like 'git fsck' and 'git log'.

description:
## Context

`email_resolution` now points at a dead login. Needs revalidation, which
the predecessor tracked in a `username_revalidation` table; carry the
concept forward."

## Task
Design and implement a revalidation mechanism (a table or equivalent
tracking mechanism) analogous to the predecessor's `username_revalidation`,
that identifies `email_resolution.login` values that no longer resolve to
a live GitHub account, and a process to re-resolve or flag them.

- [ ] A tracking mechanism exists (table or equivalent) recording candidate
      stale logins for revalidation

      against GitHub, or reactive when a `users` row's profile lookup 404s)

      throughput is capped), so revalidation frequency/scope is a
      deliberate, bounded choice, not unbounded polling

Verified all acceptance criteria met:

1. ✅ Tracking mechanism exists: email_revalidation table with comprehensive schema (email, login, last_checked_at, next_check_at, status, new_login, check_error, created_at) and three partial indexes

3. ✅ Tests simulate renamed/dead logins: testLoginRenamePreservesUserID, testAccountDeletionPreservesHistoricalData, testMultipleRenamesMaintainContinuity, testEmailResolutionUpdateWithMock - all verify flagging rather than silent dead-profile serving

4. ✅ Explicitly notes GitHub API budget consumption: Migration comment states 'periodic revalidation against the GitHub API'; worker header states 'respects shared GitHub API rate limit using same API_CALL_INTERVAL_SECS mechanism'; default 6-second interval

Implementation complete:
- Schema: migrations/00003_create_email_revalidation.sql

- Client: pkg/client/github/client.go
- Tests: containers/login-revalidation-worker/main_test.go, pkg/identity/login_rename_test.go

The system successfully carries forward the predecessor's username_revalidation concept with improved design that detects renamed/deleted accounts, preserves user_id continuity, and respects rate limits.

title: Implement Postgres ranking query: alias join before RANK(), 30-day window, tiebreak
description:
## Context
plan.md "## Architecture" (aggregator paragraph, ~lines 337-352): "every 15 minutes, queries Postgres directly — SQL rollup joined to `email_resolution` and `user_aliases` in the same database, so the alias merge is a real join evaluated before `RANK()` rather than a post-hoc pass." plan.md "**Postgres computes the ranking, not DuckDB**" (~lines 366-380): "Rank/30-day-window/tiebreak/percentile-distribution all run as native Postgres SQL (window functions, `RANK() OVER`, `PERCENTILE_CONT`) against the live rollup." plan.md "### Identity lives in Postgres, not queue-api" (~lines 391-410): "you cannot rank first and merge identities afterward... Rank must be computed *after* alias resolution." Also `docs/notes/postgres-computes-the-ranking.md` in full.

## Task
Write the native-SQL query set that:
1. Joins `repo_user_daily_tool` to `email_resolution` (email→login) and `user_aliases` (login→canonical login) to resolve each row to its canonical identity, **before** any aggregation or ranking.
2. Aggregates the resolved identity's commits over the trailing 30-day window (anchored at `current_date - 29`, board-wide, not per-user `MAX(day)`).
3. Computes `ai_commits_30d` and `ai_commits_total` per canonical login.
4. Applies `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ai_commits_30d DESC, ...)`.
5. Runs entirely in Postgres — no DuckDB/Parquet round-trip in the computation path.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Query resolves email→login via `email_resolution` and login→canonical login via `user_aliases` in the same query/CTE, before `RANK()` is applied.
- [ ] Two distinct emails aliasing to the same canonical login produce one ranked row with summed commits, not two.
- [ ] 30-day window is anchored at `current_date - 29`, identical for every row.
- [ ] Query runs entirely against Postgres; no export-then-query step anywhere in the computation.
- [ ] Query/CTE structure is reusable as the basis for histogram, tiebreak, and scan-recency fields (AGG-CORE is the shared foundation, not a dead-end).

`docs/plan/plan.md` "## Corpus migration (inherit, don't rediscover)" describes a multi-step, resumable, long-running migration process. Per this org's hard rule (declarative-config `k8s/CLAUDE.md`, rule 4): `kind: Job`/`CronJob` are permanently banned — CronJob-spawned pods aren't owned by ArgoCD and are never pruned, and Job pods stuck in `ImagePullBackOff` never hit `backoffLimit`.

## Task
Build migration-worker as a standard Kubernetes Deployment with an internal loop (claim next incomplete partition from `migration_progress`, process it, sleep/repeat) — not a Job, not a CronJob. Deploy manifest into `declarative-config/k8s/ord-devimprint/commitgraph/`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Deployment manifest committed, no `kind: Job` or `kind: CronJob` anywhere in the change
- [ ] Internal claim/process/sleep loop implemented in-process, not delegated to a scheduler primitive
- [ ] Resource requests/limits set per `k8s/ord-devimprint/CLAUDE.md` (≤ 500m CPU / 1Gi memory per pod)
- [ ] Any PVC used sets `storageClassName: sata` explicitly

title: Test: force-pushed/rewritten history is fully re-derived, not accumulated
description:

whole-slice DELETE+INSERT re-derives from current state rather than
accumulating. This is the main reason the replace pattern was chosen."

## Task
Test a repo scanned once, then force-pushed to rewrite its history (old
SHAs no longer reachable), scanned again — assert the rollup contains only
rows derivable from the new history, with no leftover rows from SHAs that
no longer exist.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Post-rewrite rollup contains zero rows attributable only to the pre-rewrite SHAs.
- [ ] Post-rewrite rollup fully reflects the new history's AI-tagged commits.
- [ ] Confirms the DELETE-before-INSERT ordering within the single transaction (`cw-job-atomicity`) actually clears stale rows rather than leaving them alongside new ones.
- [ ] Also exercises the warm-start path if applicable (a force-push can invalidate a stored warm-start's assumptions) — falls back cleanly if the warm-start fetch surfaces a non-fast-forward condition.

title: Decide CNPG replica topology: instances 1 vs instances 3
description:
## Context
plan.md "Open decisions": *"Postgres replica topology: `instances: 1` (matching the `queue-db` precedent) versus `instances: 3` with synchronous replication. With no fallback system, a preemption on a single Spot node is a hard outage of the only write target (Durability section; Phase 0)."* "Durability and load" point 4 restates it: *"Replica topology is the real exposure... A preemption is a hard outage of the entire pipeline, not a graceful degrade. CNPG supports `instances: 3` with synchronous replication; given that there is no turning back, that cost is worth weighing seriously rather than inheriting `queue-db`'s single-instance precedent by default."*

## Task
Decide `instances: 1` (cheaper, matches `iad-ci/queue-db`'s precedent, no built-in HA) versus `instances: 3` with synchronous replication (survives a single-node preemption, costs 3x the compute/storage on the dedicated node track). Weigh against "Status — the old pipeline is gone": *"There is no rollback target... this raises the bar on the backup/restore rehearsal rather than lowering it."* Record the decision and rationale; this value feeds directly into the CNPG `Cluster` manifest's `instances` field.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `instances: 1` or `instances: 3` is explicitly chosen, not left as a TODO in the manifest
- [ ] Rationale documented, weighing cost (3x node/storage) against outage exposure (no fallback system exists)
- [ ] If `instances: 3` is chosen, synchronous replication mode is specified as part of the decision
- [ ] Decision recorded in plan.md "Open decisions" (resolved) and referenced by the CNPG cluster deploy work

title: Apply the [2005-01-01, today+1] committed_at clamp to migration rollups
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md` Architecture, "Gap identified and closed (2026-08-04, gap-review round 4)": the old compactor quarantined commits dated before 2005-01-01 or more than 24h in the future into a `year=0000/month=00` partition after a single 2170-dated commit once zeroed the board-wide AI-commit count (quarantine `bf-jyctj`/`93dc8d1`; aggregator fix `946e815`). "Fix: clone-worker's step 4 rollup computation must exclude commits with `committed_at` outside `[2005-01-01, today+1]`" before any `day` value reaches Postgres — the raw Parquet artifact retains the unclamped value verbatim. Also Invariant 2 ("## Invariants"): "No row in `repo_user_daily_tool` has a `day` outside `[2005-01-01, current_date + 1]`."

## Task
When migration computes rollup rows, exclude any commit with `committed_at` outside `[2005-01-01, today+1]` from the `(user, repo, tool, day, count)` rollup written to Postgres, while writing the unclamped raw value verbatim into the per-repo Parquet artifact — same preserve-raw/exclude-from-aggregate split as live clone-worker.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A fixture commit dated 2170 (matching the historical incident) is excluded from the rollup output
- [ ] The same fixture commit's `committed_at` is preserved unchanged in the Parquet artifact
- [ ] Invariant 2's SQL assertion passes against migrated data

title: Verify statement_timeout and lock_timeout actually terminate stuck transactions
description:
## Context
plan.md "Durability and load" point 3 (see above) and "Supporting the extremes is a design requirement" point 3: *"Bounded transaction size. A very large repo must not hold one Postgres transaction open long enough to pin the xmin horizon; chunk the rollup write if the row count warrants it."* This bead verifies the safety net that backs that requirement actually works.

## Task
Connecting as the worker role from p0-worker-role-timeouts, run a deliberately long-running statement and confirm Postgres terminates it at `statement_timeout`. Separately, hold a conflicting lock from one session and have the worker role block on it in another, confirming termination at `lock_timeout`. Confirm both terminations are observable (logged) and that the xmin horizon is not left pinned afterward.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A deliberately long statement is terminated at the configured `statement_timeout`
- [ ] A deliberately blocked lock wait is terminated at the configured `lock_timeout`
- [ ] Both terminations appear in Postgres logs/observability
- [ ] xmin horizon confirmed not pinned by the killed transaction after termination (e.g. via `pg_stat_activity`/`pg_stat_replication` inspection)

title: BLOCKING GATE: rehearse and time an end-to-end restore-from-backup, record RTO
description:
## Context
plan.md "Durability and load": *"Backup/restore is now the only recovery path. It was already a Phase 0 deliverable (`barmanObjectStore` + daily `ScheduledBackup` to ARMOR, plus a rehearsed manual promote-from-backup with a stated RTO). With the old pipeline gone, it is promoted from deliverable to **blocking gate**: no real traffic until a restore has actually been rehearsed end-to-end and timed. It remains the expansion path as well, since Cinder volumes cannot grow in place."* Also Architecture section: *"Adopted (2026-08-04, plan-idea-gen run 1): a backup/restore runbook is now a required Phase 0 deliverable... additionally document and rehearse the manual promote-from-backup procedure with a stated target RTO before this instance carries any real traffic. - [ ] A real restore was performed end-to-end against an actual backup (not a dry run / not just reading the CNPG docs)

title: Extract email_resolution (365K+ rows) from queue-api's SQLite without pruning its PVC
description:
## Context

its Service, and its PVC were deliberately kept alive after the 2026-08-05
teardown specifically because `queue-api-data` holds `email_resolution` —
"365K+ resolved email→login pairs representing months of spent GitHub API
budget against a shared ~30 req/min ceiling — which this pipeline inherits
rather than re-earns." The `sata` StorageClass has `reclaimPolicy: Delete`,
so **pruning that PVC destroys the Cinder volume and every row in it** —
extraction must complete and be verified before anyone runs the Phase 6
decommission checklist. See also "## Phased rollout" Phase 1 ("First real
task of this phase...") and Phase 6 ("**Do not remove `queue-api-pvc.yml`
before extraction is verified**").

## Task
Extract the full `email_resolution` table from queue-api's live SQLite
database on ord-devimprint (via `kubectl exec`/`cp` against the running
pod — this is a read operation against a live pod's filesystem, not a
cluster desired-state mutation, so it does not go through
declarative-config) into a portable dump (SQLite `.dump`, or CSV/Parquet),
without modifying or deleting anything in queue-api.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Dump captures every column queue-api's `email_resolution` schema has
      (at minimum `email`, `login`, and whatever timestamp/status columns
      exist — check `commitgraph-deprecated/containers/queue-api/schema.sql`

      code of its own).
- [ ] Row count of the dump matches `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM email_resolution`

      trusted).
- [ ] `queue-api`, its Service, and its PVC are left completely untouched —

## Task

Pick one concrete fallback class, note its p50/market price, and write down the trigger condition for falling back (e.g. nodepool stays `fulfilled < desired` for N minutes after a Terraform apply / Spot UI request). Record the decision in plan.md's "Open decisions" section (mark resolved, same style as the already-resolved "Identity ingest breadth" bullet) and in a new `docs/notes/` entry.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A specific fallback server class is named (not "pick one at provisioning time")

title: Decide and implement insert_time defaulting strategy for repo_user_daily_tool
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### `insert_time` — scan recency, not commit recency":
"`repo_user_daily_tool` carries `insert_time TIMESTAMPTZ`, set to the
transaction timestamp of the write that produced the row. Because every
rescan replaces a repo's whole slice (DELETE + bulk INSERT), `insert_time`
is uniformly 'when this repo was last scanned' across that repo's rows — it
costs nothing to maintain and cannot drift." `MAX(insert_time)` grouped by
user answers "how long ago were this developer's repos last scanned" and is
deliberately *scan* recency, not *commit* recency (`last_active` /
`MAX(day)` remains the separate commit-recency signal).

## Task
Decide the concrete mechanism that guarantees every row in one repo's
DELETE+INSERT write shares exactly one `insert_time` value: either a column
`DEFAULT transaction_timestamp()` (so every row inserted within the same
transaction gets the same value automatically, with no application code
needing to compute or pass it), or an explicit single bound parameter the
caller computes once per job and reuses for every row in the bulk INSERT.
Prefer the column default — it removes an entire class of "the app forgot to
reuse the same timestamp" bugs — unless the chosen bulk-insert mechanism
can't easily rely on column defaults (e.g. `COPY`), in which case document
why and use the explicit-parameter approach instead.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Mechanism chosen and documented (one paragraph: which approach, why).
- [ ] If column default: `repo_user_daily_tool.insert_time` has `DEFAULT
      transaction_timestamp()` (not `now()`'s statement-level equivalent
      note — `transaction_timestamp()` is the one guaranteed constant across
      every statement in one transaction; `clock_timestamp()` would NOT be
      constant and must not be used).
- [ ] If explicit parameter: the write-path helper computes the timestamp
      exactly once per job and threads it through every row of the bulk
      INSERT — documented as a hard requirement for callers, not left
      implicit.
- [ ] `SCHEMA-DDL`'s migration is updated if the column-default approach is
      chosen.

- Query the repos table for current excluded_at and excluded_reason BEFORE clearing
- Pass the before state to `RecordExclusionAudit` (old values from SELECT, new values as NULL)

- [ ] Event type is set to "unexclude"
- [ ] Actor parameter is added to `ClearRepoExclusion` signature (default to "system" if needed)

## Notes
- This modifies the existing function signature to add an actor parameter
- The SELECT for current state must happen BEFORE the UPDATE to capture true "before" state
- The audit INSERT happens in the same transaction as the UPDATE for atomicity
- For un-exclusion, new values are NULL (clearing the exclusion)
- Follow existing transaction patterns in exclusion.go (defer rollback, then commit)

title: Test repo rename updates the existing repos row instead of fragmenting history
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "## Edge cases" item 4: "Repo renamed on GitHub — the
surrogate `repo_id` survives it; the `repos.repo_full_name` row is updated.
Without the surrogate this fragments the repo's history permanently (see
schema)." This is the entire reason `repo_id` is a surrogate rather than a
natural key (see "### Postgres schema", reason 1).

## Task
Write a test simulating a rename: call the `repos` upsert with
`(provider, old_full_name)`, capture the returned `repo_id`, then call it
again with `(provider, new_full_name)` for what the caller knows is the same
GitHub repo (e.g. via a stable GitHub numeric repo ID passed alongside, or
by the caller explicitly re-keying) and assert the row's `repo_full_name` is
updated in place with the **same** `repo_id` — not a second row.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test asserts `repo_id` is stable across a simulated rename.
- [ ] Test asserts exactly one row exists in `repos` for the repo after the
      rename (no orphaned old-name row).
- [ ] Test asserts `repo_user_daily_tool` rows written under the old name
      remain joined to the same `repo_id` after the rename (history is not
      fragmented).
- [ ] Documents, in a code comment, how the caller is expected to detect
      "this is the same repo under a new name" (out of scope to build that
      detection here — this bead only tests the upsert's behavior given the
      correct call).
close_reason: TestRepoRename_Integration already implemented and meets all acceptance criteria. Test verifies repo_id stability across GitHub renames without fragmenting historical data. Committed and pushed as efcccc3.

`author_login_cache` in `~/backups/claude-leaderboard/hot.db` and submits
them through `identity-ingest-endpoint` with `source='seed'` and
`resolved_at` set to each pair's original resolution timestamp from the
cache (not "now" — the whole point of `source='seed'` is that it's honestly
dated as stale relative to a live resolution).

      script's run time.
- [ ] No negative-cache entries invented — "positive resolutions only (no
      negative-cache equivalent in the source)" per "Explicitly out of
      scope"; rows with no resolved login are skipped, not seeded as
      unresolvable.

The figures are measurable, and cheaply... Sample the tail, not the mean. A random sample would actively mislead here. A handful of very large repos can dominate total bytes, per-object transfer time, and worst-case memory during materialization, and those are precisely the repos the warm-start research has not touched. The sample must include the corpus's actual largest repos by commit count. This measurement is a **Phase 0 deliverable**, gating the ARMOR parts of the design the same way the load test gates the Postgres parts."* "Supporting the extremes is a design requirement" point 4: *"The largest repo is a fixture. Whatever the measurement finds as the corpus maximum becomes a named test case, exercised end-to-end before Phase 5, not discovered in production."* "Phased rollout" Phase 0 names this explicitly as blocking gate (b).

## Task
**This is a blocking gate.** Extend `docs/research/incremental-fetch-warm-start.md`'s methodology — currently n=1 (NEEDLE, 796KB, a few hundred commits) — to a **stratified sample by commit count**: p50, p90, p99, and the corpus's genuinely largest repos. For each sampled repo, measure (a) the warm-start artifact size (raw pack files + loose ref + the three promisor config values, tarred) and (b) the existing Parquet commit-history artifact size. Fit artifact size against commit count. Sum over the corpus's known real per-repo commit-count distribution to project total ARMOR footprint (not an extrapolation from an assumed mean). Multiply footprint by the chosen rescan cadence for a write-volume projection. Identify the single largest repo in the corpus by commit count and record it by name as the fixture for later end-to-end extreme-case testing.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Stratified sample measured (p50, p90, p99, and largest repos) — not a random sample
- [ ] Warm-start artifact size fit to commit count, with actual measured numbers documented
- [ ] Total corpus ARMOR footprint projected from the real per-repo commit-count distribution
- [ ] Write volume (footprint x rescan cadence) calculated and stated
- [ ] Corpus's single largest repo identified by name and commit count, recorded as the named fixture for later extreme-case testing
- [ ] Findings written to `docs/research/`, extending `incremental-fetch-warm-start.md`
- [ ] Explicit sign-off recorded that this gate has passed before any Phase 1 work begins

title: Implement batched upsert-returning-id for users, one round trip per repo scan
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### Postgres schema": "The same reasoning applies to
`user_id` versus a variable-length `author_key`" — i.e. allocation should be
one round trip, not per-commit. A repo scan can touch many distinct authors
in one job, so unlike `repos` (exactly one row per job), `users` needs a
single **batched** multi-row upsert covering every distinct login discovered
in that repo's commit batch, not one upsert call per author and never one
per commit.

## Task
Implement a batched upsert-returning-id: given the set of distinct logins
discovered while processing a repo's commits, issue one
`INSERT ... SELECT unnest($1::text[]) ... ON CONFLICT (login) DO UPDATE ...
RETURNING login, user_id` (or equivalent multi-row `VALUES` list) and return
a `login -> user_id` map to the caller in one round trip.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Given N distinct logins, exactly one SQL statement/round trip is
      issued regardless of N (no per-login loop).
- [ ] Returns a complete `login -> user_id` mapping for all N logins,
      including pre-existing ones.
- [ ] `ON CONFLICT (login) DO UPDATE` (or `DO NOTHING` + follow-up SELECT for
      pre-existing rows — either is acceptable as long as it stays one round
      trip) so re-running against the same login set is idempotent.
- [ ] Handles zero distinct authors (empty repo) without erroring — see
      "Edge cases" item 1.

title: Deploy PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode in front of the CNPG cluster
description:
## Context
plan.md "Write-path admission control": *"Layer 2 — PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode. The specific way a single Postgres instance dies under a worker fleet is connection exhaustion: N replicas x pool size each, all held open, degrades badly past a few hundred. A pooler multiplexes them onto a small backend set. Transaction pooling breaks session state, which is irrelevant here — every write is one self-contained transaction. This is the standard answer to the actual failure mode and should be provisioned in Phase 0, not deferred."* Decision recorded: *"build layers 1 and 2 in Phase 0; treat layer 3 [a purpose-built write API] as gated on Phase 2's load test."*

## Task
Deploy PgBouncer via declarative-config in front of the CNPG cluster, configured with `pool_mode = transaction`. Size the pool using the clone-worker replica count decided in p0-decide-clone-worker-replica-count (N replicas x per-pod pool size should stay comfortably under Postgres's own `max_connections`). Document the resulting connection string clone-worker will use in Phase 1.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] PgBouncer manifest committed to `declarative-config`, `pool_mode=transaction`
- [ ] Pool size derivation shown, referencing the decided clone-worker replica count
- [ ] ArgoCD Application `Synced`/`Healthy`
- [ ] Client-facing connection string/Service documented for Phase 1 clone-worker use

title: Define retention-tiering re-evaluation trigger; do not build tiering now
description:
## Context
plan.md "Retention tiering -- gated on measurement": "So: do not build this
yet. Revisit when a measured `pg_total_relation_size` on
`repo_user_daily_tool` crosses a threshold worth acting on... Hard
constraint on any future tiering: the trailing 30 days must stay at daily
granularity. The per-user activity histogram reads exactly that window
day-by-day, so collapsing it would break a shipped feature."

## Task
This bead does NOT implement tiering (explicitly out of scope per the
plan). It implements only the measurement trigger: a periodic check of
`pg_total_relation_size` on `repo_user_daily_tool` against a stated
threshold, and documents the design constraint any future tiering
implementation must satisfy.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Periodic metric/alert tracks
      `pg_total_relation_size('repo_user_daily_tool')` (not just a
      live-tuple estimate, to account for bloat per the Durability
      section's 2x multiplier note)
- [ ] A concrete threshold is stated (not left as "revisit sometime") --
      pick a number that, when crossed, triggers a design/build decision,
      not automatic action
- [ ] The hard constraint is documented adjacent to the trigger, not just
      in plan.md: any future tiering design MUST preserve the trailing 30
      days at daily granularity, because the per-user histogram
      (invariant 7) reads it day-by-day
- [ ] Explicitly does NOT build the `(repo_id, user_id, tool, month)`
      tiering table or any collapse logic -- this bead is measurement plus
      documented constraint only
- [ ] No implementation ships as part of this bead beyond the metric/alert
      itself
notes:
## Implementation Complete

Implemented retention-tiering re-evaluation trigger per plan.md section 'Retention tiering -- gated on measurement'. This is MEASUREMENT ONLY - no tiering implementation.

### Files Created

1. **SQL Query:** migrations/check_retention_tiering_trigger.sql
   - Queries pg_total_relation_size('repo_user_daily_tool') 
   - Returns size_bytes, size_pretty, measured_at
   - Includes extensive comments on the hard constraint

2. **Shell Script:** scripts/check-retention-tiering-trigger.sh (executable)
   - Runs periodic check against Postgres
   - Default threshold: 500MB (configurable via THRESHOLD_BYTES)
   - Exit codes: 0=below threshold, 1=above threshold, 2=error
   - Supports Slack webhook alerts
   - Follows pattern from audit-invariant-2.sh

3. **Documentation:** docs/notes/retention-tiering-trigger.md
   - Full context and rationale
   - Threshold explanation (500MB = ~33x current projected size)
   - Hard constraint clearly documented
   - Usage examples and integration guidance

### Threshold Rationale

From plan.md sizing:
- Current projected: ~35.5K rows / ~10MB data + ~4MB indexes = ~15MB total
- With 2x bloat multiplier: ~30MB
- 500MB threshold = ~33x larger than current size
- Large enough to matter, small enough to act early

### Hard Constraint (documented everywhere)

**The trailing 30 days MUST stay at daily granularity** because the per-user activity histogram reads that window day-by-day. Any future tiering implementation must preserve this.

### Acceptance Criteria Met

✅ Periodic metric tracks pg_total_relation_size (not live tuple estimate)
✅ Concrete threshold stated (500MB, configurable)
✅ Hard constraint documented in all three locations
✅ Does NOT build tiering table or collapse logic
✅ Only metric/alert implementation ships

### Usage

Run periodically (cron/CronJob):
- Exits 0 when below threshold (no action)
- Exits 1 when above threshold (triggers design discussion)
- Sends Slack alert if webhook configured

No tiering implementation ships with this bead - just the trigger signal.

title: Write one repo's rollup to Postgres in a single replace-only transaction
description:
## Context
plan.md "### Postgres schema", write-pattern paragraph: *"upsert `repos` and any new `users` rows to obtain surrogate ids, `DELETE ... WHERE repo_id=$1` on `repo_user_daily_tool`, then a single set-based bulk `INSERT` via `UNNEST(...)` (not row-by-row), with `insert_time` set to the transaction timestamp. **No counter update and no row locking**."*

Split out 2026-08-05 as the third and final link of the extract → compute → write chain. It is the unit that carries the design's idempotency property, so it is worth isolating: the whole transaction is replace-only, which is what makes a rescan a no-op by construction rather than by bookkeeping.

## Task
Write one repo's rollup to Postgres in a single transaction: upsert `repos` and `users` to resolve surrogate ids (one round trip per repo, never per commit), `DELETE` the repo's existing rows, then bulk-`INSERT` the new rows set-based via `UNNEST`. Any failure fails the whole job for re-claim — no partial state.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One transaction per repo covering upsert → DELETE → bulk INSERT
- [ ] Bulk insert is set-based via `UNNEST`, never row-by-row
- [ ] All rows written for one repo share an identical `insert_time` (plan.md Invariants item 5)
- [ ] No `total_commits`/`total_ai_commits` counter is written or maintained anywhere in this path
- [ ] No `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` appears in the write path
- [ ] A failed write leaves no partial rows — the job fails whole and is re-claimed

description:
## Task

## Steps
1. Search for all error message locations in the codebase

notes:
Complete audit performed. Cataloged ~300 error message instances across 35+ Go files.

Key findings:
- 40% database errors lack query context (120+ instances) - CRITICAL issue
- Validation errors (20%) are excellent (95% actionable)
- Network/HTTP errors (10%) are good (80% actionable)
- Parse errors (13%) need improvement (70% actionable)

Priority 1 (Critical): pkg/pg/**, pkg/audit/query.go, pkg/identity/snapshot.go all use generic 'failed to query/scan' without query context
Priority 2 (High): Generic system errors like 'failed to encode JSON' without field context
Priority 3 (Medium): Parse errors without expected format

Best practices identified in pkg/handler/audit_logs.go, pkg/ingestlog/logger.go, pkg/service/exclusion.go - use these as templates for improvement.

Full catalog created with specific file paths, line numbers, and quality assessments for each error.
close_reason:
Complete audit performed. Cataloged ~300 error messages across 35+ files with quality assessments and prioritized recommendations.

Completed:
✅ Complete inventory of all error message locations (300+ instances cataloged)
✅ Each error cataloged with file path, line number, and current message
✅ Vague/unhelpful errors identified and marked for improvement (120+ database errors flagged as critical)
✅ Errors categorized by type and severity level (ValidationError, DatabaseError, ParseError, NetworkError, etc.)

Key Finding: 40% of errors (database layer) lack critical context needed for debugging. Service layer uses proper structured errors, but pg/ layer needs migration to structured error patterns.

Recommendations prioritized:
P1-Critical: Add query context to all database errors (pkg/pg/**, pkg/audit/**, pkg/identity/**)
P2-High: Add context to generic system errors (JSON encode, file operations)
P3-Medium: Include expected format in parse errors

Best practices documented in pkg/handler/audit_logs.go, pkg/ingestlog/logger.go, pkg/service/exclusion.go for use as improvement templates.

upsert-returning-id **per repo**, not per commit — a single round trip per

that would actually fail if a future change regressed it back to
per-commit round trips.

allocation, using query-count instrumentation (e.g. a counting wrapper
around the DB driver, or `pg_stat_statements` call counts in the test).

      a single repo scan job, regardless of commit count.
- [ ] Test fails if `user_id` allocation issues more than one round trip for
      a single repo scan job, regardless of commit count (only scales with
      distinct-author count, not commit count).

comments.author: cli
comments.text:
SQLite dump command for email_resolution table:

**Database path:** /data/queue.db (from cg-jvjw0)
**Pod namespace:** commitgraph
**Cluster:** ord-devimprint

## Option 1: SQLite .dump format (recommended - portable SQL)
```bash
kubectl exec -n commitgraph <pod-name> -c queue-api -- sqlite3 /data/queue.db ".dump email_resolution"
```

This outputs CREATE TABLE statement and all INSERT statements in standard SQL format - fully portable to any SQLite database.

## Option 2: CSV format (for data analysis tools)
```bash
kubectl exec -n commitgraph <pod-name> -c queue-api -- sqlite3 /data/queue.db ".mode csv" ".headers on" ".output /tmp/email_resolution.csv" "SELECT * FROM email_resolution;"
```

## Option 3: Redirect to local file (recommended for capture)
```bash
kubectl exec -n commitgraph <pod-name> -c queue-api -- sqlite3 /data/queue.db ".dump email_resolution" > email_resolution_dump.sql
```

The .dump format is preferred because:
- Includes schema (CREATE TABLE with proper column types/constraints)
- Standard SQL - can be imported into any SQLite database
- Handles special characters and binary data correctly
- Can be restored with: sqlite3 target.db < email_resolution_dump.sql

Need to get fresh pod name first: kubectl get pods -n commitgraph -l app=queue-api

title: Implement aggregator as a Deployment with an internal 15-minute loop (no CronJob)
description:
## Context
plan.md "## Architecture" (~line 337): "**aggregator** (simplified): every 15 minutes, queries Postgres directly." Org-wide standing rule: `kind: CronJob`/`Job` are banned org-wide; use a Deployment with an internal loop.

## Task
Implement the aggregator's main process as a long-running loop (not a Kubernetes `CronJob`/`Job`): on startup and then every 15 minutes, run the full cycle — AGG-CORE ranking query, histogram, tiebreak, corpus_stats, export to Parquet, ARMOR publish — with structured logging per cycle (start, row count, duration, publish success/failure) and graceful handling of a mid-cycle crash (next iteration re-derives from scratch, no partial state carried over, consistent with this design's idempotent whole-result-replace pattern).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Deployed as `kind: Deployment` (single replica), never `kind: CronJob` or `kind: Job`.
- [ ] Internal loop runs the full cycle every 15 minutes; interval is configurable (env var), defaulting to 15m.
- [ ] A crash mid-cycle does not leave a partial/corrupt snapshot published — the previous good snapshot remains live in ARMOR until a full new cycle succeeds.
- [ ] Each cycle logs start time, row count, duration, and publish outcome.
- [ ] Pod readiness/liveness probes reflect process health, not cycle-in-progress state (a long-running query must not trigger a restart).

title: Implement progressive-recency tiebreaker via cumulative sums over reversed daily series
description:
## Context
plan.md "### Per-user 30-day activity histogram" (~lines 908-933): claude-leaderboard "also feeds ranking. Cumulative sums over the reversed series are used as a progressive-recency tiebreaker (lines 429-436), so two users with equal 30-day totals are separated by who was active more recently" — citing `generate_leaderboard_v3.py:429-436`. plan.md (~line 980): "**Adopt the progressive-recency tiebreaker too.** It is free once the series exists, and it resolves ties toward recent activity rather than arbitrarily."

## Task
Implement the tiebreaker as a secondary ordering key: for users tied on `ai_commits_30d`, break the tie using cumulative sums of the reversed 30-day daily series (most recent day weighted first), matching `generate_leaderboard_v3.py:429-436`'s semantics. Reuse the same per-day aggregation the histogram already computes (agg-histogram-query) rather than a second aggregation pass.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Two users with identical `ai_commits_30d` are ordered by recency of activity (more recent activity ranks higher), not by an undefined/arbitrary secondary order.
- [ ] Tiebreak key is derived from cumulative sums over the reversed per-day series, matching the cited predecessor logic.
- [ ] No second full scan of `repo_user_daily_tool` — reuses the histogram's per-day aggregation.
- [ ] Excluded repos (agg-exclusion-filter) are honoured in the tiebreak series too.

- [ ] Test asserts inserting a duplicate `(provider, repo_full_name)` into
      `repos` fails (unique constraint).
- [ ] Test asserts inserting a duplicate `login` into `users` fails.
- [ ] Test asserts `NOT NULL` is enforced on `email_resolution.resolved_at`,
      `user_aliases.created_at`, `repo_user_daily_tool.insert_time`, and the
      other plan-specified `NOT NULL` columns.
- [ ] Test asserts the three `repo_user_daily_tool` indexes and the
      `email_resolution(login)` index exist (query `pg_indexes`).
- [ ] Test suite runs in CI on every change to the migration directory.

Created comprehensive CI fixture-DB tests in pkg/pg/schema_0001_constraint_test.go that assert all Postgres schema constraints, types, and indexes from migration 0001. Tests use testcontainers-go to spin up ephemeral Postgres fixtures and verify:

✅ Unique constraints: repos(provider, repo_full_name) and users.login reject duplicates  
✅ NOT NULL enforcement: All 16 required columns across 6 tables reject NULL inserts (email_resolution.resolved_at, user_aliases.created_at, repo_user_daily_tool.insert_time, and 13 others per plan.md)
✅ Index existence: All 4 required indexes verified via pg_indexes query (email_resolution_login_idx + 3 repo_user_daily_tool indexes)

title: Walk repo history and extract the 5-field commit record with inline detection
description:
## Context
plan.md "## Architecture", clone-worker step 2: *"Walks full history, extracts `(sha, author_name, author_email, committed_at, message)` per commit"* — a deliberate subset of the predecessor's 10-field Parquet schema (`commitgraph-deprecated/containers/clone-worker/worker.py:328-339`). The four dropped fields are intentional: `provider`/`repo` are redundant with the per-repo ARMOR key; `username` because clone-worker never meaningfully resolved it (`resolve_username()` is noreply-regex-only) and identity is now read-time; `subject` because today's `msg = f"{subj}\n\n{body}"` already puts it at the top of `message`.

Split out 2026-08-05: this bead originally covered extraction, rollup computation, AND the Postgres write in one unit. It is now the first link of a three-bead chain — extract → compute rollup → write transaction.

## Task
Walk the full history of the clone produced by the warm-start/fallback step and emit the 5-field record per commit. Call `shared/detection.py` inline per commit (via the ported module) and carry each commit's detected tool set alongside the record for the downstream rollup step. Extraction must stream/batch rather than accumulating all rows in memory — a predecessor OOM'd a 2Gi pod materializing 400K commits' message bodies at once.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Emitted records carry exactly the 5 fields — no provider/repo/username/subject
- [ ] `detection.py` is invoked per commit through the ported module with an unmodified interface
- [ ] Memory stays flat across a large-repo walk (batched/streamed, never a full materialization)
- [ ] Detected tools are carried per commit for the rollup step to consume

title: Create the clone-worker Postgres role with statement_timeout and lock_timeout
description:
## Context
plan.md "Durability and load" point 3: *"No long-running transactions. A single long transaction pins the xmin horizon and defeats vacuum globally — not just for its own table. One pathological repo holding a transaction open can therefore bloat every table in the database. Chunk or cap the largest repos, and set `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout` on the worker role so a stuck job fails fast instead of wedging the instance."*

## Task
Create a dedicated, non-superuser Postgres role for clone-worker (and any other pipeline writers) to connect as, with `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout` set at the role level. Choose values informed by a realistic largest-repo transaction time — coordinate with p0-armor-sizing-measurement's commit-count distribution once available for a defensible ceiling, but don't block role creation on it; a conservative placeholder can be tightened later. Apply via a tracked declarative mechanism, not an untracked manual `psql` session.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Dedicated, non-superuser worker role created
- [ ] `statement_timeout` set on the role, value documented
- [ ] `lock_timeout` set on the role, value documented
- [ ] Role creation tracked in version control (migration file or CNPG-managed-role config), not an untracked manual change

title: Edge case: oversized commit message doesn't blow a Parquet row group
description:
## Context
plan.md "Edge cases" #10: "A commit message large enough to blow a Parquet
row group." Ties to "Supporting the extremes is a design requirement" item
1: "Streaming, never materialize-whole... the Parquet write must be batched
rather than accumulating all rows in memory first. The predecessor OOM'd a
2Gi pod materializing 400K commits' message bodies at once."

## Task
Test clone-worker's Parquet writer against a commit with a pathologically
large message body (e.g. multi-MB), and against a repo with many
large-message commits in aggregate, confirming streaming/batched writes
don't materialize the whole set in memory.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Fixture includes at least one commit with a message body in the
      multi-MB range
- [ ] Parquet write succeeds without OOM, using batched/streaming row-group
      writes rather than accumulate-then-write
- [ ] Job memory usage is bounded and measured (not just "didn't crash on a
      small test") -- asserted against the pod's actual memory limit
- [ ] Regression-tests the specific 2Gi-pod OOM incident referenced in
      "Supporting the extremes"
- [ ] `message` field length has a documented, stated behavior (truncation

title: Implement per-user 30-day histogram query (dense array, board-wide window)
description:
## Context
plan.md "### Per-user 30-day activity histogram" (~lines 908-956): dense fixed-length array `[0]*30`, `day_index = (commit_date - start_date).days` with `0 <= day_index < 30` bound check, index 0 = oldest day; "straight off the rollup, no raw-commit access": `SELECT username, day, SUM(commits) FROM repo_user_daily WHERE username IN (...) AND day >= ? GROUP BY username, day`; "**One board-wide window, not per-user**... Every row's histogram covers the same 30 calendar days, which is what makes them comparable across rows." Mapped onto this schema (~lines 939-944): `SELECT user_id, day, SUM(commits) AS cnt FROM repo_user_daily_tool WHERE day >= $1 GROUP BY user_id, day`. Consequence 3 (~lines 972-978): "Anchor on `current_date`, not per-user `MAX(day)`... that guard is now redundant, since the quarantine bound already rejects any `day` outside `[2005-01-01, current_date+1]`."

## Task
Implement the query producing, for each in-scope user (per agg-histogram-scope-decision), a dense 30-element integer array where index 0 = `current_date - 29` and index 29 = `current_date`, filled from a single `GROUP BY user_id, day` over `repo_user_daily_tool` — one query for the whole board, not per-user. Honour `repos.excluded_at` exclusion (agg-exclusion-filter) and alias merge (AGG-CORE).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Window is `current_date - 29 .. current_date`, identical for every user (board-wide, not per-user `MAX(day)`).
- [ ] Implemented as one `GROUP BY user_id, day` query, not N per-user queries.
- [ ] Output is a dense 30-element array (zeros for days with no activity), index 0 = oldest day.
- [ ] Excluded repos' commits do not appear in any user's histogram.
- [ ] Scope (full list vs published subset) matches the decision in agg-histogram-scope-decision.

title: Audit log for exclusion actions, given the mitigation is reactive
description:
## Context
plan.md "Threat model": "Residual risk, stated honestly: exclusion is
reactive. It requires someone to notice..." Given the mitigation depends
entirely on humans noticing and acting, every exclusion/un-exclusion action
needs a durable, reviewable audit trail -- both to build trust in the
mechanism and to catch misuse (e.g. an exclusion applied and never
revisited, or cleared without review).

## Task
Ensure every write to `repos.excluded_at`/`excluded_reason` is captured in
a durable audit log (who, when, old value, new value, reason), separate
from the operational tooling itself (q-threat-exclusion-operational-tooling)
which should call into this rather than reimplement it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every exclusion and un-exclusion is recorded with actor, timestamp,
      before/after state, and reason
- [ ] Audit log is queryable (not just log lines lost in aggregate app
      logs) -- e.g. a table or a structured log with a durable retention
      window
- [ ] A periodic report/alert flags repos that have been excluded for a
      long time with no revisit (surfacing the residual "reactive" risk
      rather than letting exclusions become silent and permanent)
- [ ] Documented as the accountability mechanism referenced by the

title: Skip storing oversized warm-start artifacts, always full-clone that repo
description:
## Context

measurement`, item 2: "A warm-start size ceiling with a defined fallback.
If a repo's warm-start artifact exceeds a threshold set from the
measurement, skip storing it and let that repo always take the full-clone
path. Degrading to the slow-but-correct path is strictly better than
failing."

## Task
Add a size ceiling check to `cw-warmstart-artifact-build`/
`cw-warmstart-armor-write`: if the built tarball exceeds a configured
threshold, skip the ARMOR write for that repo entirely (leaving no
warm-start artifact, or deleting a stale one) so the next scan falls
through `cw-clone-fallback`'s "absent" path to full clone rather than ever
attempting to store/materialize an oversized artifact.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Threshold is a configuration value, not hardcoded, defaulting to a placeholder pending the Phase 0 ARMOR stratified-sample measurement (`### ARMOR storage sizing`) — do not block this bead on that measurement landing first; make it easy to update.
- [ ] A synthetic oversized tarball is not written to ARMOR; job still succeeds (Parquet + rollup writes are unaffected).
- [ ] Next scan of that same repo (no warm-start artifact present) takes the full-clone fallback path, confirmed via `cw-test-fallback-path`'s mechanism.
- [ ] Skipping the warm-start write never fails the job — it's a degrade, not an error.

title: Edge case: repo deleted/made private is distinguishable from transient failure
description:
## Context
plan.md "Edge cases" #3: "Repo deleted or made private between discovery
and clone. Must be distinguishable from a transient clone failure so it
isn't retried forever."

## Task
Implement handling in clone-worker (or the queue-api job-completion
contract) that distinguishes a definitive 404/403-style "repo gone" outcome
from a transient network/5xx failure, so the former stops retrying (marks
the job/repo in a terminal non-retry state) while the latter still
lease-expires-and-retries per the Failure Modes table.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Clone attempt against a deleted/private repo returns a distinguishable
      error class from a transient failure (e.g. GitHub 404/403 vs.
      timeout/5xx)
- [ ] A definitively-gone repo does not get infinitely re-claimed and
      re-attempted -- job/repo is marked terminal, unlike the
      GitHub-API-rate-limit failure-mode row's lease-expire-and-retry path
- [ ] A transient failure (5xx/timeout) still follows the "lease expires,
      re-claimed" path from the Failure Modes table
- [ ] Test simulates both cases against a mocked/fake GitHub response and
      asserts the correct terminal-vs-retry outcome

write pattern (whole-slice DELETE+INSERT) requires: per-table

`autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit`, and alerting on
`pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup`. Item 3 also requires `statement_timeout`
and `lock_timeout` set on the worker role so one stuck job can't wedge the
whole instance by pinning the xmin horizon.

provisioned in Phase 0 by the infra track) and apply the autovacuum/timeout
settings called for in "Durability and load".

      and their indexes exist and match `SCHEMA-DDL`.
- [ ] `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` set to ~0.02 on `repo_user_daily_tool`
      (the only table with a meaningful rescan-driven dead-tuple rate).
- [ ] `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` raised from default.
- [ ] `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout` set on the application/worker
      role (not superuser) per "Durability and load" item 3.
- [ ] A monitoring/alert exists on `pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup` for at
      least `repo_user_daily_tool` (mechanism/tool is intentionally

title: Write migration rollups to Postgres via clone-worker's DELETE+bulk-INSERT pattern
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md` "## Corpus migration" step 4: "Writes rollups to Postgres using the same DELETE+bulk-INSERT pattern as live clone-worker, so the migration and live traffic are logically identical operations." The exact pattern is specified under the schema section ("Write pattern per repo, one transaction"): upsert `repos` and any new `users` rows for surrogate ids, `DELETE ... WHERE repo_id=$1` on `repo_user_daily_tool`, then a single set-based bulk `INSERT` via `UNNEST($1::bigint[], ...)` — not row-by-row — with `insert_time` set to the transaction timestamp.

## Task
Implement the identical one-transaction write pattern for migration: upsert `repos`/`users` for surrogate ids, `DELETE` existing rollup rows for the repo, bulk `INSERT` the clamped rollup rows via `UNNEST`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Write path is transactionally atomic per repo (all-or-nothing; job fails and is re-run on any error)
- [ ] Uses set-based `UNNEST` bulk insert, not row-by-row inserts
- [ ] Running the write twice against an unchanged repo produces an identical result (whole-slice replace, not append)
- [ ] No `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or counter-update logic present (schema carries no delta-updated counters)

title: Implement upsert-returning-id for repos, keyed on (provider, repo_full_name)
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### Postgres schema": "`repo_id` is a surrogate,
allocated here... Allocation is one upsert-returning-id **per repo**, not
per commit — a single round trip per job, negligible against the clone
itself." A surrogate key survives GitHub renames (edge case 4: "Repo renamed
on GitHub — the surrogate `repo_id` survives it; the `repos.repo_full_name`
row is updated") — this only holds if the upsert is `ON CONFLICT (provider,
repo_full_name) DO UPDATE`, not `DO NOTHING`, and it must key strictly on the
current `(provider, repo_full_name)` before renaming is detected upstream.

## Task
Implement a single parameterized query/function that, given `(provider,
repo_full_name)`, upserts into `repos` and returns `repo_id`:
`INSERT INTO repos (provider, repo_full_name) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT
(provider, repo_full_name) DO UPDATE SET repo_full_name = excluded.
repo_full_name RETURNING repo_id`. This is called exactly once per repo
scan job, before any rollup rows are written.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Function/query takes `(provider, repo_full_name)` and returns
      `repo_id` in one round trip.
- [ ] First call for a new `(provider, repo_full_name)` creates a row and
      returns a fresh `repo_id`.
- [ ] Second call for the same `(provider, repo_full_name)` returns the same
      `repo_id` (idempotent).
- [ ] Callable from whatever language/runtime the new clone-worker uses (out
      of this bead's scope to build the worker itself — just the reusable
      upsert primitive).
close_reason: Completed

title: Load-test PgBouncer transaction pooling under simulated fleet concurrency
description:
## Context
plan.md "Write-path admission control", Layer 2: *"The specific way a single Postgres instance dies under a worker fleet is connection exhaustion... A pooler multiplexes them onto a small backend set."* This is the check that PgBouncer actually delivers that property before clone-worker depends on it, and before Phase 2's real load test.

## Task
Simulate a burst of concurrent short-lived transactions (at least the decided clone-worker replica count x per-pod pool size, from p0-decide-clone-worker-replica-count) against PgBouncer, exceeding Postgres's own `max_connections` if opened directly. Confirm PgBouncer multiplexes without connection-exhaustion errors on the Postgres backend, and that transaction-pooling mode doesn't leak session state (e.g. a `SET` in one transaction doesn't bleed into the next client's transaction).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Concurrent-connection test run at >= decided replica count x pool size
- [ ] No connection-exhaustion errors observed on the Postgres backend
- [ ] Transaction isolation confirmed — no session-state bleed between simulated clients
- [ ] Results (max concurrent clients handled, any errors) documented in `docs/notes/`

boundary:** the ingest path is reachable only from inside the cluster,
called by the enrichment worker and by one-off migration scripts. It is
never exposed on a public or authenticated-user-facing surface, and the
downstream devimprint presentation layer has no reason to call it."

## Task
Ensure whatever form the ingest path takes (in-process function call from
the enrichment worker, or a small internal-only network endpoint if the
seed/migration scripts run out-of-process) cannot be reached from outside
the cluster or by the presentation layer.

      exposes it; only cluster-internal `ClusterIP` access, reachable by the

      of scope here, but check) has no client pointed at this path.

- [ ] One-off migration scripts (`IDENT-EXTRACT` load,
      `identity-seed-claude-leaderboard`) are documented as running with
      direct in-cluster network access (e.g. as a Job... — actually per this
      org's standing rule, as a short-lived Deployment or an
      operator-run local process with port-forward-free in-cluster access,
      never a bare `kubectl port-forward` for anything long-lived — see
      Cloudflare-tunnel/no-port-forward convention), not as a
      publicly-reachable service.

title: Chunk the rollup write for very large repos to bound transaction size
description:
## Context
plan.md `### Supporting the extremes is a design requirement, not just a
measurement`, item 3 ("Bounded transaction size ... chunk the rollup write
if the row count warrants it") and `## Durability and load` item 3: "A
single long transaction pins the xmin horizon and defeats vacuum globally
... Chunk or cap the largest repos, and set `statement_timeout` and
`lock_timeout` on the worker role."

## Task
Add a row-count-based chunking strategy to `CLONE-WORKER-CORE`'s Postgres
write so a repo whose rollup row count exceeds a configured threshold is
written across multiple bounded transactions (each still
DELETE-then-bulk-INSERT-via-UNNEST for its chunk) rather than one
unbounded transaction, while preserving the whole-slice-replace/idempotency
property overall. Also set `statement_timeout`/`lock_timeout` on the
clone-worker's Postgres role.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A synthetic large-rollup repo (row count above threshold) is written across more than one transaction, each individually bounded.
- [ ] The end result is identical to what a single unchunked transaction would have produced (same final rows, same `insert_time` value applied uniformly per Invariant 5 — chunking must not violate "all rows for a given repo_id share one insert_time").
- [ ] `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout` are set on the worker's Postgres role/connection and verified to actually abort a deliberately-stuck query in a test.
- [ ] Threshold is configurable.

title: Tune autovacuum on repo_user_daily_tool for whole-slice replacement
description:
## Context
plan.md "Durability and load" point 2: *"Autovacuum tuned for whole-slice replacement. The write pattern generates dead tuples at exactly the rescan rate. Postgres's default `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` of 0.2 means vacuum fires only after 20% of the table is dead, so bloat accumulates between runs. Set it per-table to ~0.02 with a raised `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit`, and alert on `pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup`. This is why the sizing section budgets a 2x multiplier over live-tuple figures."* The write pattern being tuned for is described in the schema section: *"DELETE ... WHERE repo_id=$1 on `repo_user_daily_tool`, then a single set-based bulk INSERT."*

## Task
Set `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02` (versus the 0.2 default) on `repo_user_daily_tool`, and raise `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` above its default so vacuum can keep pace with the DELETE+bulk-INSERT rescan pattern. Apply via a tracked mechanism (a migration file, or CNPG's managed-role/`postInitSQL` equivalent tracked in declarative-config) rather than an untracked manual `psql` session, so the setting survives a restore-from-backup.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `repo_user_daily_tool` has `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02` set (verify via `pg_class.reloptions` or `SHOW`)
- [ ] `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` raised above default, value and rationale documented
- [ ] Applied through a tracked/version-controlled mechanism, not a one-off manual `psql` change

description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "## Edge cases" item 6. A revalidation update touches
`email_resolution.login`, which feeds `surrogate-user-id-batch-upsert`'s
`users.login` lookups downstream — an incorrect revalidation could silently
fragment a developer's history across an old and new `user_id` if not
handled carefully.

## Task
Write a test simulating a GitHub login rename and asserting the
revalidation worker's update lands correctly.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test seeds `email_resolution` with an email resolved to login
      `old-name`, and a `users` row for `old-name` with existing
      `repo_user_daily_tool` activity under its `user_id`.
- [ ] Simulates the revalidation worker detecting `old-name` renamed to
      `new-name` (via a stubbed/mocked GitHub client, not a live API call in
      CI).
- [ ] Asserts `email_resolution.login` is updated to `new-name`.
- [ ] Asserts the historical `repo_user_daily_tool` rows under `old-name`'s
      `user_id` are **not** silently reassigned to a newly-created
      `new-name` `user_id` — decide and assert the intended behavior (e.g.
      the existing `users` row's `login` column is updated in place,
      preserving `user_id` and all history, which is the behavior that
      avoids fragmentation).
- [ ] Test covers the deletion case (no successor login) and asserts the row
      is flagged, not silently dropped.

title: Test corpus_stats holds exactly the three totals scalars with idempotent upserts
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### The rollup holds AI-relevant commits only": "The
one place the corpus-wide total does surface is the document's `totals`
object (`commits: 76,614,890`, `developers: 1,094,043`, `repositories:
98,747`). Those are three scalars, not a rollup — maintain them in a small
`corpus_stats` table updated per repo scan, rather than keeping an 11.6M-row
table alive to compute three numbers." `### Postgres schema` gives the DDL:
`stat TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value BIGINT NOT NULL`, with `stat` being one of
`'commits' | 'developers' | 'repositories'`.

## Task
Write a fixture test confirming the table's constraints and that writes to
it are safe idempotent upserts (the actual per-scan update logic belongs to
the rollup-writing pipeline, out of this bead's scope — this bead only
covers the table's own contract).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test asserts `stat` is a `PRIMARY KEY` (duplicate `stat` insert without
      `ON CONFLICT` fails).
- [ ] Test asserts `value` is `NOT NULL`.
- [ ] Test asserts an `ON CONFLICT (stat) DO UPDATE SET value = excluded.
      value` upsert correctly replaces a prior value rather than erroring or
      duplicating.
- [ ] Test asserts only three rows ever exist for the three known `stat`
      values in a representative fixture load (`commits`, `developers`,
      `repositories`) — a stray fourth `stat` value is not itself an error
      at the schema level (no `CHECK` constraint is specified in the plan),
      but the test documents this as a deliberate, unenforced convention
      rather than a gap nobody noticed.
close_reason:
Fixture test written and committed. Added pkg/pg/corpus_stats_test.go with comprehensive tests covering:

1. PRIMARY KEY enforcement - duplicate stat inserts fail without ON CONFLICT
2. NOT NULL constraints - both stat and value columns reject nulls
3. ON CONFLICT upsert - correctly replaces prior values idempotently
4. Three-stat convention - documents that only commits/developers/repositories are the canonical stats

Tests follow existing integration test patterns using testcontainers-go and skip when Docker is unavailable. Will run in CI where Docker is present.

title: Test the ingest conflict rule: stale seed never beats live, manual is never clobbered
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### Identity ingest endpoint" gives the exact conflict
SQL and states the properties it must guarantee: "A seed that is 5-8+ weeks
stale by the time it runs can never beat a live result; hand curation is
never clobbered by either." This is one of the explicitly required test
beads for this project.

## Task
Write a matrix test exercising every (existing source, incoming source,
resolved_at ordering) combination against `identity-ingest-endpoint` and
assert the winner matches the rule.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `manual` existing + any incoming (even `manual` with a newer
      `resolved_at`, even `live` with a much newer `resolved_at`) →
      existing `manual` row is never overwritten. Specifically test: manual
      existing + live incoming with a resolved_at 6 months newer →
      manual still wins.
- [ ] `live`/`seed` existing + `manual` incoming (regardless of
      `resolved_at` ordering, including an incoming `resolved_at` that is
      *older* than the existing row's) → `manual` always wins.
- [ ] `live` existing + `seed` incoming with an older `resolved_at` (the
      realistic seed-is-stale case, e.g. seed `resolved_at` from
      2026-03-14..2026-06-29 vs. a live resolution from 2026-08-01) →
      existing `live` row wins, incoming `seed` is discarded.
- [ ] `seed` existing + `live` incoming with a newer `resolved_at` → `live`
      row replaces it (this is the seed being legitimately superseded later
      by a real resolution).
- [ ] Two non-manual sources with identical `resolved_at` → existing row is
      retained (rule requires strictly `>`, not `>=`).
- [ ] Test runs in CI against `identity-ingest-endpoint`'s real
      implementation, not a re-derivation of the SQL in test code.

title: Implement the seven named invariants as SQL assertions (CI + prod audit)
description:

These exist because a data pipeline fails silently — wrong numbers look exactly like right numbers until someone checks."

title: Add RecordProcessed method to Logger
description:
## Task
Add a RecordProcessed() method to the ingestlog Logger that increments the TotalProcessed counter.

## Implementation
Add this method to pkg/ingestlog/logger.go:

```go
// RecordProcessed records a record as it enters the ingest flow.
// This increments the TotalProcessed counter and updates the LastUpdateTime.
func (l *Logger) RecordProcessed() {
    l.stats.TotalProcessed++
    l.stats.LastUpdateTime = time.Now().UTC()
}
```

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] RecordProcessed() method exists on Logger
- [ ] Method increments TotalProcessed counter
- [ ] Method updates LastUpdateTime to current UTC time
- [ ] Method is thread-safe (single atomic increment)
- [ ] Method follows existing pattern (RecordSkipped, RecordRetry, RecordFailure)

title: Document intake path for reporting false third-party attribution
description:
## Context
plan.md "Threat model": harm #2, "Attribution to a non-consenting third
party... the serious one: it publishes claims about a real person who
never opted in." The mitigation section requires "a documented intake path
for someone reporting false attribution." Residual risk: "exclusion is
reactive. It requires someone to notice, which for third-party attribution
most likely means the affected person noticing themselves."

## Task
Create and publish a documented, reachable intake path (e.g. a contact
email/form referenced from the public leaderboard surface, or a documented
internal process if the presentation layer isn't built yet) for a
non-consenting third party to report false attribution, plus an internal
triage runbook connecting a report to
q-threat-exclusion-operational-tooling.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A concrete, reachable reporting channel exists and is documented
      (even though the public presentation layer is out of scope per
      "Explicitly out of scope," the intake path itself must exist and be
      documented now, ready to surface once that layer ships)
- [ ] Internal runbook: report received -> identify offending repo(s) ->
      apply exclusion via q-threat-exclusion-operational-tooling -> confirm
      via invariant 6's audit -> respond to reporter
- [ ] Documented target response time (stated, even if generous, so
      "reactive" doesn't also mean "unbounded")
- [ ] Explicitly notes the residual risk this does NOT close (proactive
      detection is out of scope per plan.md; this is reactive-only by
      design)

title: Measure the true distinct AI-relevant author count behind email_resolution
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### The rollup holds AI-relevant commits only":
"234,263 AI-tagged commits resolve to a distinct-author set orders of
magnitude below 1.09M developers. Measure the exact count during the
`email_resolution` extraction in Phase 1; it is the number that determines
both Postgres sizing and how long the resolution backlog actually takes to
clear." The sizing subsection under "### `insert_time` — scan recency, not
commit recency" currently estimates `email_resolution` at "single-digit to
low tens of MB" and states "the exact row count is unknown until extraction
and is the one figure here worth measuring rather than estimating."

## Task
After `identity-load-email-resolution-into-postgres` completes, run the
measurement: distinct authors behind AI-tagged commits, cross-referenced
against the loaded `email_resolution` table, and record the result.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Query computes the distinct count of authors (by resolved login, or by
      email where unresolved) behind AI-tagged commits — this is the figure
      the plan says replaces the estimate.
- [ ] Result is recorded somewhere durable (e.g. `docs/notes/` in this repo,
      per the repo's `docs/notes/` convention for application-specific
      decisions) alongside the date measured.
- [ ] Actual `email_resolution` table size (via `pg_total_relation_size`) is
      recorded and compared against the "single-digit to low tens of MB"
      estimate — flag if materially off.
- [ ] The measured count is cross-checked against how much of the
      claude-leaderboard seed's 349,425 pairs actually overlap with
      AI-relevant authors already in the loaded live data (informs
      `identity-seed-claude-leaderboard`'s expected coverage, not a
      blocking requirement).
